channel.title: Medical Xpress - latest medical and health news stories
channel.description: Medical Xpress internet news portal provides the latest news on science including: Physics, Nanotechnology, Life Sciences, Space Science, Earth Science, Environment, Health and Medicine.

item.title: ACAAI: Considerable delay seen from Rx to approval for children's biologics
item.description: There is a considerable delay from prescription of biologic therapy to final approval for pediatric patients, and almost 40% of prescriptions requiring a prior authorization (PA) are denied, according to a study presented at the annual meeting of the American College of Allergy, Asthma and Immunology, held from Nov. 12 to 16 in Phoenix.

item.title: No oxygen? Chicken brain cells still survive
item.description: Without oxygen, brain cells die within minutes … or do they? When it's a chicken brain, Wake Forest University researcher Lara do Amaral-Silva has found, the answer is no.

item.title: US set to lose measles-free certification
item.description: This week, the United States will lose its designation as a country where measles has been eliminated, as an outbreak of the dangerous, highly contagious disease keeps spreading.

item.title: Researchers find potential way to protect the brain from HIV and opioid damage
item.description: People living with HIV continue to struggle with memory loss, difficulty concentrating and poor decision-making, even as antiretroviral treatments have dramatically improved life expectancy. For patients who also use opioids—which may be prescribed to manage the chronic pain that can accompany HIV—these cognitive problems can be even worse. Until now, scientists haven't understood exactly why.

item.title: Liver cells activate scarring-linked genes in stiff surroundings but favor repair signals in softer conditions
item.description: Soft and stiff extracellular matrix environments influence how hepatic stellate cells (HSCs) respond during liver injury. Researchers from Science Tokyo investigated how matrix stiffness shapes the direction of HSC activation. They revealed that soft conditions favored regeneration-associated cellular states, while stiff conditions promoted fibrosis-associated gene expression.

item.title: Daytime brain waves resembling deep sleep could explain hallucinations in Parkinson's disease
item.description: Parkinson's disease is a progressive brain disorder that damages dopamine-producing neurons, causing symptoms to worsen over time. The disease is associated with motor difficulties that can manifest as tremors, stiffness, poor balance and slow movements. However, the disease reaches beyond movement, affecting how people think, perceive the world around them and sleep. Caregivers and health care workers often report that cognitive decline, excessive daytime sleepiness (EDS) and perceptual distortions add to the burden of the disease and can take the greatest toll on quality of life.

item.title: Scientists identify likely cause of typhoid fever's deadliest complication
item.description: Typhoid fever is an ancient scourge that remains all too deadly in the developing world today. And while it has been described in detail for more than a century, the reasons for its lethality have never been understood. Yale researchers now have an answer.

item.title: CAR T-cell therapy shows promise for patients with lupus
item.description: For patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR T-cell) therapy is associated with consistent reductions in disease activity, according to research presented at the annual meeting of the American College of Rheumatology (ACR Convergence 2026), held from Nov. 6 to 11 in Orlando, Florida.

item.title: The body clock keeps ticking, but activity and body temperature become less coordinated in aging mice
item.description: Physical activity and body temperature fluctuate throughout the day according to biological rhythms. In addition to the ~24-h circadian rhythms, these physiological processes display shorter rhythms with periods of several hours, known as ultradian rhythms. However, it remains unclear how these rhythms change with age and how those changes relate to the master circadian clock of the brain.

item.title: From supply chains to cancer research: How causal AI is opening new research paths
item.description: How can automotive supply-chain research inform a new line of inquiry in cancer treatment research? For Constructor University Lecturer and Postdoctoral Researcher Ishansh Gupta, the answer is causal AI—a form of artificial intelligence that goes beyond simple pattern recognition to analyze why certain patterns exist, and help predict outcomes of changes.

item.title: First results published from the largest brain atlas ever created
item.description: Imagine trying to understand a city without a map. You see buildings and meet people, but you have no idea how everything is connected. Researchers face a similar challenge when studying the brain. That is why international scientists within the Brain Initiative Cell Atlas Network are working together to create an atlas that maps all types of human brain cells. The first results have now been made publicly available.

item.title: Treating iron deficiency: The everyday factors that affect how your supplements work
item.description: Iron deficiency is the most common nutritional deficiency worldwide, affecting around 2 billion people. Yet many people may not even realize they have low iron for months or even years.

item.title: A possible new approach for treating autism and conditions caused by a single faulty gene copy
item.description: Researchers at UCLA Health have shown in lab-grown human brain cells that boosting the activity of a healthy gene copy can offset the effects of a mutation linked to autism. The findings, published in Nature Neuroscience, suggest a new direction for treating autism and related neurodevelopmental conditions, though the work is still at an early stage.

item.title: HIV prevention education brought into Baltimore beauty shops through community-designed program
item.description: What if a conversation about HIV prevention began not in a doctor's office but in a neighborhood beauty shop?

item.title: Astaxanthin supplements: What the science says about skin, exercise and your brain
item.description: Smoother skin, sharper eyesight, better memory, stronger joints, improved athletic performance and even protection against aging—astaxanthin is marketed as a supplement with an extraordinary range of health benefits. But how much of this promise is backed by evidence in people?

item.title: This time, the virus is on the patient's side. AI helped design it
item.description: AI can write emails, create seasoning blends or put pets in Renaissance outfits. One adventurous baker used ChatGPT to concoct a cake from sauerkraut and seaweed. Now, there's an AI-made virus on the scene.

item.title: Brain scans reveal two regions that shrink before the hippocampus in Alzheimer's
item.description: Johns Hopkins University researchers have identified two areas of the brain that show significant signs of Alzheimer's disease before it reaches the hippocampus, possibly providing new biomarkers that could get people diagnosed and started on treatment before symptoms begin, when interventions may be most effective.

item.title: A cancer drug is being touted online as a way to grow taller—what you need to know
item.description: A cancer drug linked to rapid growth spurts in children has caught the attention of teenagers looking to gain an extra few inches in height.

item.title: Early-life environmental factors linked to health across childhood and adolescence
item.description: Environmental exposures during pregnancy and childhood can be associated with multiple aspects of health at the same time, with many of these associations persisting into adolescence, according to a new study led by the Barcelona Institute for Global Health (ISGlobal), in collaboration with the French National Institute for Health and Medical Research (Inserm).

item.title: What's the link between ADHD medication and psychosis?
item.description: This year, several alarming reports have warned that Australians are developing psychosis from using stimulant medications, typically prescribed for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, or ADHD.

item.title: Q&A: Can the body's natural signals help wounds heal better with diabetes?
item.description: Type 1 diabetes, an autoimmune condition in which the pancreas doesn't produce enough insulin, can make it harder for wounds to heal. Researchers are exploring why and how the body's natural healing processes could be improved. Pedro Geralde, PD, a professor at the Université de Sherbrooke in Canada, shared his team's work at the American Physiological Society's 2026 Comparative Physiology conference last month. We caught up with Geralde to learn more.

item.title: Research finds a pop void in studies tracking how the brain and heart respond to music
item.description: We all know the joy of hearing a song we love. It can be a physical experience, as we tap our toes or sing at the top of our lungs. Or it can be emotional, lifting our mood or conjuring long-buried memories.

item.title: Study probes how step trackers, health apps relate to exercise levels
item.description: A new University of Mississippi study examined whether people who used modern fitness tools such as step counters, heart rate monitors and health apps are more likely to meet federal physical activity guidelines.

item.title: Early-life exposure to obesity may cause long-term immune weakness
item.description: Exposure to a high-fat diet in the womb or in early life may trigger a persistent weakness in the immune system, according to a study led by researchers at the Perelman School of Medicine at the University of Pennsylvania. The results, shown in mice but supported by observations in humans, are published in Nature Immunology.

item.title: AI-assisted imaging method advances 150-year-old technique for studying tissue
item.description: For centuries, researchers and clinicians have used microscopes to study the causes and effects of disease on tissues and help make diagnoses—the practice of histopathology. While microscopes have certainly improved, scientists still rely on tissue preparation approaches that distort subtler features and entirely remove lipids and water-soluble materials. The result is an incomplete and imperfect view that cannot capture lipid data and other details that may be relevant to disease.

item.title: Beyond DMT: Why the true power of Brazil's sacred jurema plant is social, not just psychedelic
item.description: Jurema-preta is the name of both a plant—Mimosa tenuiflora—and an Indigenous spiritual tradition of northeastern Brazil. The plant is used to make a potentially hallucinogenic brew that is consumed in sacred rituals. The exact mixture of herbs and other elements contained in the brew is a secret known only by jurema mestre shamans and never revealed.

item.title: Smoking in, vaping out: The social trend worrying health experts
item.description: Smoking is becoming more socially acceptable while disapproval of vaping is growing, new international research on social trends has found. The University of Queensland-led research studied smoking and vaping trends among almost 20,000 adults who smoked daily in Australia, Canada, England and the United States, finding vaping has become less socially accepted than smoking.

item.title: New smartphone game offers promise as added depression support for adults
item.description: Depression care doesn't have to be limited to clinics and medications. In a recent study, researchers presented a new smartphone app called Fig: The Game for Depression (or simply Fig), which is designed as a therapeutic grounded in cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) principles.

item.title: Eating without fear: A single vaccine shows promise against multiple food allergies
item.description: According to U.N. figures, more than 220 million people worldwide suffer from food allergies, which cause the body to perceive an otherwise harmless protein in food as dangerous. As a result, the immune system launches an attack on the protein, which in the worst cases can be life-threatening.

item.title: Teens who report greater parental involvement are more likely to say they would help cyberbullying victims, study finds
item.description: For parents worried about their teenagers' online lives, "How much screen time?" may not be the most important question.
